anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously burdened by inefficient application-level SQL logic, a mis-chosen optimizer execution plan, and an overwhelmed replication pipeline. Together, these three root causes inflate data access and modification volume, execute them with an overly expensive physical plan, and then replicate the excessive redo more quickly than replicas can receive or apply it.

SQL Workload Logic Anomaly: Application-issued statements or transaction scopes process far more rows, columns, or time than business logic requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer selects a markedly sub-optimal plan even though statistics are adequate, producing needless scans, joins, or memory usage.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or downstream replicas cannot consume, write, or replay the primary’s log stream at the rate it is generated, leading to lag and log-retention growth on the primary.

Combined Symptoms: • Individual statements show extreme and highly variable latency, with the same SQL text occasionally exploding into multi-second or multi-minute runtimes. • Primary nodes exhibit CPU spikes, inflated logical and physical I/O, and rapid transaction-log growth. • Replicas report widening receive/replay lag, accumulate large relay logs, serve increasingly stale reads, and may fall out of synchronous commit windows. • Application tiers observe both foreground timeouts (from slow queries) and eventual consistency anomalies (stale replica reads). • Monitoring tools reveal erratic plan-cache behavior, large gaps between estimated and actual costs, and replication performance alerts, making isolation of any single culprit difficult.

Causal Chain and Reinforcement: Inefficient SQL statements (workload logic anomaly) generate large scans, wide result sets, or unnecessarily long transactions. When the optimizer compounds this by choosing a poor plan (plan selection anomaly), resource usage and redo generation surge. The bloated and prolonged transactions emit voluminous and bursty log streams that must be shipped and applied downstream. Replicas, already limited by network bandwidth, single-threaded apply, or hardware constraints, fall behind (replication synchronization anomaly). The growing replica lag prevents timely log truncation on the primary, expanding storage pressure and lengthening recovery time objectives. Meanwhile, lagging replication can starve read-only workloads of fresh data, prompting additional load on the primary and further worsening the optimizer’s plan quality through changing cache and memory pressure. Thus the three anomalies form a feedback loop that degrades both primary performance and replication health in OLTP and mixed analytical scenarios.

entry.official_description: Replica has more GTIDs than the source has, using the source's SERVER_UUID. This may indicate that the the last binary log file was truncated or lost, e.g., after a power failure when sync_binlog != 1. The source may have rolled back transactions that were already replicated to the replica. Replicate any transactions that source has rolled back from replica to source, and/or commit empty transactions on source to account for transactions that have been committed on source but are not included in GTID_EXECUTED.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
